title: Which way to Moscow?
hook: Moscow is far east of Seattle. Which way do you set off?

knows: that long flights follow curved-looking routes on flat maps
doesNotKnow: that the starting direction of a shortest route can be far from the map direction
that a map centred on a place shows shortest routes from it as straight lines

misconception: Moscow is far east of Seattle, so you start by flying east.
objective: The learner can say that the shortest route from Seattle to Moscow starts almost due north (about 11.5° east of north) because it is a great circle over the Arctic.
keyState: East has been tried (the route misses Moscow by thousands of km) and the heading has then been turned to within 2° of 11.5°, where the drawn route reaches Moscow.

claims.text: The shortest route from Seattle to Moscow starts about 11.5° east of north.
claims.source: Initial great-circle bearing atan2(sin Δλ cos φ2, cos φ1 sin φ2 − sin φ1 cos φ2 cos Δλ) (Williams, Aviation Formulary; Movable Type Scripts; from memory) for Seattle 47.61N 122.33W and Moscow 55.76N 37.62E: 11.505°. Demo.tsx bearing(), the value the stage prints. Matches the cm-geography brief. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-13 (pass 6): Node: initial bearing 11.505 degrees.

claims.text: The shortest route from Seattle to Moscow is about 8,370 km.
claims.source: d3 geoDistance × 6,371.0088 km = 8,369.9 km on a sphere (Demo.tsx DIST_KM). The brief says 8,371 km; the 1 km difference is coordinate rounding. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-13 (pass 6): Node: 8,369.9 km.

claims.text: Setting off due east from Seattle on a great circle, the route passes about 7,940 km from Moscow.
claims.source: Demo.tsx missKm(90): minimum distance from Moscow to the first 9,500 km of the great circle leaving Seattle at 90°, sampled every 10 km: 7,938 km (builder scratch mirror). The reveal quotes it only if the learner pressed 'Face east'. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-13 (pass 6): Independent Node: minimum distance to Moscow along due-east great circle, 9,500 km at 10 km steps = 7,938 km.

claims.text: On a map centred on Seattle (azimuthal equidistant), straight lines from Seattle are shortest routes and distances from it are true.
claims.source: Snyder (1987), Map Projections: A Working Manual, USGS PP 1395, azimuthal equidistant: great circles through the centre are straight lines with true scale along them (from memory). | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-13 (pass 6): Re-derived; no issue.

claims.text: The route crosses Canada, the far north of Greenland and the Arctic Ocean, then Norway and Finland.
claims.source: Builder scratch run: d3 geoInterpolate Seattle→Moscow sampled every 0.25% against the kit's 1:110m countries: USA, Canada (incl. Arctic islands), Greenland at about 82°N, sea, Norway at 71°N 26°E, Finland, Russia. Peak latitude 82.3°N. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-13 (pass 6): Independent Node walk of the route against countries-110m: USA > Canada (with Arctic islands) > Greenland (about 82 N, north coast) > Arctic Ocean > Norway (71 N, 26 E) > Finland > Russia. Peak 82.3 N.

claims.text: Moscow lies far east of Seattle, and both are far north.
claims.source: Gazetteer coordinates (from memory): Seattle 47.61N 122.33W, Moscow 55.76N 37.62E; 160° of longitude apart. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-13 (pass 6): Longitude difference 160 degrees.

claims.text: Real flights also bend for winds and airspace.
claims.source: General aviation practice (flight planning uses wind-optimal tracks and airspace restrictions; from memory, needs a source such as an ICAO or FAA flight-planning reference). | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-13 (pass 6): Wind-optimal tracks and airspace/ATC routing are standard flight-planning practice; no named source is attached, and none is needed for a general statement.

claims.text: The same shortest route from Seattle to Moscow is a straight line on the Seattle-centred map and, on an ordinary flat map, a curve that bends north.
claims.source: Great circles are not straight on equirectangular maps; Demo.tsx draws the same great-circle points with d3-geo geoEquirectangular. Needs a check. · Fact-check pass 19 2026-10-14: VERIFIED: own slerp of the great circle peaks at 82.3 N (lon 43.9 W) between endpoints at 47.6 N and 55.8 N, with no antimeridian crossing on the 42 W-centred equirectangular map, so it is drawn as an arch bending north. | v3 2026-10-14 (demo-builder): reveal reworded to 'You saw it both ways: a straight line on the Seattle-centred map, a curve bending north on the flat map'; the gate now requires viewing the on-target route on the flat map (milestone 'flat-hit'). The locked stage now shows the flat map, not the centred one. Reopened. · Fact-check pass 21 2026-10-14: VERIFIED: Own node: initial bearing 11.5 deg; for headings 10-13 deg the 9,500 km route peaks at 81-83 N near 34 W and stays within -80..+85 deg of the 42 W map centre (no wrap), so on the equirectangular map it is an arch bending north. On the azimuthal equidistant map centred on Seattle every great circle through the centre is a straight line. The 'flat-hit' gate shows the on-target route on the flat map.

recall.question: Two cities are both far north, one far east of the other. The shortest route between them starts out heading:
options: Roughly east, toward the other city on the map
Well north of east, climbing toward the pole
recall.why: The great circle between two high-latitude cities bends over the polar region, so it starts much further north than the map direction: Seattle to Moscow starts 11.5° east of north.
